after.title: Preprint: High vaccine coverage and non-pharmaceutical interventions decreased hospitalizations and deaths due to the Omicron variant in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada
after.authors: Anokye, F.; Li, M. W.; Hurford, A.
after.abstract: The Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador (NL) had high vaccination coverage, and few infections were reported prior to the establishment of the Omicron variant. We investigated whether changes in the timing and rate of booster dose administration could have reduced severe disease outcome and reliance on non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) during the Omicron wave in NL. We used a vaccination-stratified epidemiological model calibrated to serology data to investigate the impact of vaccination relative to counterfactual vaccination strategies under actual, strict and no NPI scenarios. Compared with a Canadian vaccination rate scenario, the actual vaccination rollout in NL was estimated to have prevented approximately 519 hospitalizations and 122 deaths from December 15, 2021 to December 15, 2022, corresponding to reductions of 25.9\% and 30.9\%, respectively. These reductions reflected contributions from NL's higher initial primary series coverage (81.3\%), higher final booster dose coverage (57.3\%), and the implementation of various NPIs for 89 days after the Omicron BA.1 variant became established. Earlier and faster administration of booster doses reduced the duration of strict NPIs required to achieve hospitalization targets. Our findings show how the timing and rate of vaccination rollout can complement NPIs to reduce severe disease and the duration for which strict NPIs are required.

after.abstract: ABSTRACT Background: Malignant effusions are clinically accessible yet underutilized sources of metastatic tumor cells. However, abundant background immune cells complicate tumor cell isolation and molecular characterization. We integrate AI-powered single-cell imaging and morphology-guided label-free tumor cell enrichment with genomic profiling to characterize phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity in malignant effusions. Methods: We applied a pre-trained deep learning model to brightfield images of single cells from malignant effusions of 10 patients with metastatic breast cancer to extract morphological features, quantify tumor cell fraction (TCF), and guide label-free microfluidic enrichment. Conclusion: AI-powered analysis leverages single-cell morphology for tumor cell identification and label-free enrichment, while integration with genomic profiling enables simultaneous interrogation of phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity in malignant effusions. after.authors: Kwong, J. C.; Goldfarb, D. M.; Bhatt, M.; Xie, J.; Buchan, S. A.; Papenburg, J.; Cheng, J.; Eltorki, M.; Finkelstein, Y.; Sabhaney, V.; Pernica, J. M.; Gravel, J.; Kam, A.; Berthelot, S.; Burstein, B.; Emsley, J.; Mater, A.; Ali, S.; Shah, A.; Poonai, N.; Beer, D.; Gill, P.; Dickinson, J.; Freedman, S.
after.abstract: Importance: Influenza causes substantial morbidity in children, yet Canadian data on influenza vaccine effectiveness (VE) in preventing emergency department (ED) visits and hospitalizations are limited. Objective: To estimate VE against influenza-associated ED visits and hospitalizations among children during the 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 seasons. Design: Test negative case control design. Setting: Fourteen Canadian pediatric tertiary-care hospitals participating in the Surveillance Program for the Rapid IdeNtification and TracKing of Infectious Diseases in kidS (SPRINT KIDS) network. Participants: Symptomatic children aged 6 months to <18 years tested for influenza from October 27, 2024, to June 7, 2025, and from November 2, 2025, to June 13, 2026. Exposure: At least one dose of current season influenza vaccine. Main Outcomes and Measures: VE against laboratory confirmed influenza A or B associated with an ED visit or hospitalization. VE was estimated using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, epidemiologic week, site, and high-risk comorbidity. Results: The 2024/2025 season included 17,316 encounters (median [IQR] age=41.0 [18.5, 82.3] months; 54.0% male), with 4,760 influenza-positive cases (8.9% vaccinated) and 12,556 influenza-negative controls (15.9% vaccinated). The 2025/2026 season included 13,417 encounters (median [IQR] age=33.5 [16.7, 74.8] months; 54.1% male), with 4,798 cases (7.6% vaccinated) and 8,619 controls (18.1% vaccinated). VE against any influenza was 47% (95%CI, 40%, 53%) and 53% (95%CI, 46%, 59%) in 2024/2025 and 2025/2026, respectively. VE against ED visits was 53% (95%CI, 45%, 59%) and 57% (95%CI, 49%, 63%), and VE against hospitalization was 33% (95%CI, 16%, 47%) and 48% (95%CI, 33%, 59%) in 2024/2025 and 2025/2026, respectively. VE was lower against influenza A as compared to B in both seasons: 31% (95%CI, 22%, 39%) vs. 75% (95%CI, 64%, 82%) (p<0.001) in 2024-2025; and 42% (95%CI, 32%, 50%) vs. 64% (95%CI, 55%, 72%) (p=0.001) in 2025/2026. VE was lower in children aged 10 to <18 years than in those <10 years, particularly among children with comorbidities. Protection against influenza A lasted up to 90 days, whereas it persisted beyond 120 days for influenza B. Conclusions and Relevance: Influenza vaccines were moderately effective against pediatric ED visits and hospitalizations in both seasons. Routine vaccination should continue to be recommended to prevent hospital-attended influenza.

after.title: Preprint: Medication history, not clinical profiles, predicts antihypertensive treatment persistence across health systems
after.authors: Wang, S.; Lu, D.; Tao, T.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Pharmacy, South China Hospital of Shenzhen University
after.abstract: Background. Hypertension control remains poor worldwide, in large part because patients discontinue antihypertensive treatment. Machine-learning (ML) prediction models for medication persistence are typically single-country and cross-sectional, rarely compared with simple clinical information, and lack external validation across health systems. Methods. We harmonized three prospective aging cohorts -- the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS), the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), and the US Health and Retirement Study (HRS) -- including adults aged >=50 years with doctor-diagnosed hypertension at baseline and known medication status at follow-up. We used baseline plus two prior waves to predict non-use of any antihypertensive medication at the next wave (treatment non-persistence), with 21 harmonized cross-sectional features, 11 longitudinal history features (including the prior non-use ratio), and a 3-feature parsimonious medication-history score (baseline non-use, prior non-use ratio, prior discontinuation). Models were L2-regularized logistic regression and random forest, evaluated by 5-fold x 5-repeat nested cross-validation and by direct transport of a CHARLS-trained model to SHARE and HRS without retraining. Three simple rule-based comparators were prespecified: baseline carry-forward (T0), prior non-use count (T1), and the 3-feature score (T2). Non-inferiority of T2 versus the full 32-feature logistic model was tested at delta=0.03 AUC. Country-level external validation across 18 SHARE countries used random-effects meta-analysis and inverse-variance meta-regression on World Bank indicators. Results. The analytic samples comprised 4,532 (CHARLS), 26,128 (SHARE) and 9,495 (HRS) participants, with non-persistence of 22.8%, 19.1% and 12.6%. Within each cohort, adding medication history raised AUC from 0.59-0.67 to 0.78-0.85 (Delta AUC 0.17-0.20; all 95% CIs >0). On direct transport, history models retained AUC 0.73-0.76 in SHARE and 0.83-0.85 in HRS, whereas cross-sectional models collapsed to near chance in SHARE (AUC 0.55-0.57). The baseline carry-forward rule alone achieved AUC 0.70-0.80; the 3-feature score achieved 0.75-0.83 and was non-inferior to the full logistic model (Delta AUC <=0.027; upper CI bounds <0.03) in all three within-cohort comparisons and both transport targets. Across 18 European countries, cross-sectional models pooled at 0.55 (I^2=30%) while history models pooled at 0.74-0.76 (I^2=82-88%); transported AUC increased with national wealth (r=0.58, P=0.011), and calibration slope declined with non-persistence burden (r=-0.69, P=0.002) and out-of-pocket expenditure share (r=-0.51, P=0.032). Conclusions. A parsimonious medication-history core transfers across health systems, whereas cross-sectional clinical profiles do not. Complex ML adds little beyond a one-question or three-variable medication-history rule. Discrimination is strongest in high-resource, low-burden systems, but probability calibration degrades where non-persistence is common, requiring local recalibration before individual-level use.

after.authors: Eggerstorfer, B.; Altmann, P.; Murgas, M.; Ponleitner, M.; Godbersen, G. M.; Klöbl, M.; Unterholzner, J.; Silberbauer, L. R.; Vraka, C.; Philippe, C.; Nics, L.; Hahn, A.; Hacker, M.; Gryglewski, G.; Lanzenberger, R.
after.abstract: Immune dysregulation is implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), but its links to clinical features and in vivo brain phenotypes remain uncertain. We examined ten plasma biomarkers in 36 unmedicated MDD patients and 48 control participants using high-sensitivity immune profiling at baseline, alongside PET/MR imaging of brain serotonin transporter (SERT) binding and regional structural measures. Patients underwent three months of antidepressant treatment and were followed up with MR imaging. Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) was higher in MDD patients ({beta} = 0.66, 95% CI 0.22 - 1.11), and interleukin-33 (IL-33) correlated with subcortical volumes across all participants ({beta} = 0.22, 95% CI 0.07 - 0.38). No marker correlated with SERT binding or cortical thickness after correction, and neither SERT binding nor brain structural measures differed by diagnosis. In the longitudinal analysis, interleukin-13 (IL-13) was associated with greater antidepressant response during first-line treatment with escitalopram ({beta} = 1.09, 95% CI 0.56 - 1.61). IL-15 and IL-13 showed nominal associations with hippocampal volume increase after treatment. These findings suggest astroglial involvement in MDD and that peripheral immune states relate to subcortical brain structure. IL-13 is a candidate prognostic marker of response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Its tentative association with longitudinal changes in hippocampal volume suggests that immune processes in MDD may be related to both the capacity for clinical improvement and brain structural plasticity during treatment.

after.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of serial biosampling and environmental exposure assessment in reproductive-aged men and compare participant experiences with in-person versus remote sample collection. Design: Prospective cohort pilot study. Subjects: Eighteen healthy men aged 21 to 44 years with no history of infertility, medical conditions or medications known to cause infertility, or prior scrotal or testicular surgery. Exposure: Indoor and personal environmental exposure monitoring using PurpleAir monitors and Fresh Air wristbands, respectively. Main Outcome Measures: Feasibility of repeated remote semen and blood collection, evaluated by participant retention and number of samples returned, and participant-reported acceptability, ease of use, discomfort, preference for at-home versus in-clinic sampling, and willingness to participate in longitudinal studies. Results: 18 participants completed the initial in-person and scheduled at-home sampling, and 16 (89%) completed subsequent remote sampling. Participants successfully collected and shipped serial capillary blood samples using homeRNA and semen samples using the Fellow Semen Analysis Kit. Participants rated both collection methods as easy to use and reported minimal discomfort with blood collection. At-home participation was preferred over in-clinic sampling, particularly for semen collection. All 16 participants completing the final survey reported willingness to participate in a similar study again. Participants were willing to provide a median of 18 semen samples (range, 2-40) and 18 blood samples (range, 5-40) over a future hypothetical study. Both home-based environmental monitoring approaches were well accepted. Conclusion: Serial remote semen and blood collection paired with environmental exposure monitoring was feasible and acceptable among reproductive-aged men. High retention, preference for at-home sampling, and willingness to provide repeated samples support this approach for larger longitudinal studies investigating environmental exposures and male reproductive health.

after.title: Preprint: PRISM-AD quantifies clinical and genetic contributions to cognitive risk prediction
after.authors: Dai, Y.; Wood, C. S.; Jiang, X.; Hsu, Y.-C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston
after.abstract: Background: Older adults with high inherited Alzheimer's disease (AD) susceptibility can still be cognitively normal (CN). An overall risk estimate alone does not show the cognitive and genetic contributions within a forecast. Objective: To quantify clinical and genetic contributions to cognitive prognosis. Methods: PRISM-AD combined nonlinear clinical functions and a polygenic risk score (PRS) term in 4,435 European-ancestry participants. Participant-level internal validation evaluated first recorded mild cognitive impairment (MCI) after CN in 908 participants and AD dementia after MCI in 714, within three or five years. Separately fitted comparators used identical inputs. Post hoc clinical-course comparisons used regression with robust standard errors and Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) correction. Results: PRISM-AD using current assessments achieved average precision of 0.2996 and 0.4094 for three- and five-year CN-to-MCI, with estimates close to logistic regression. No PRISM-AD PRS increment met BH q < 0.05. Three-year first-MCI forecasts characterized risk contributions in 893 initially CN participants. A retrospective comparison over available follow-up included 95 participants with later AD and 701 with CN at their last diagnostic assessment. Modeled genetic factors were higher in later AD in nine of ten shared cognitive-risk deciles. After adjustment for modeled cognitive risk and fold, the genetic-factor ratio was 1.135 (nominal 95% CI, 1.073 to 1.201, BH q < 0.001). Conclusions: Higher genetic contributions were associated with later AD at comparable modeled cognitive risk. These exploratory profiles require independent validation before use in cognitive follow-up or prevention research.

after.abstract: Background: The landmark genome-wide association meta-analysis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and AD-by-proxy across N = 2,815,127 individuals (Uffelmann et al., Nature, 2026) expanded the known susceptibility landscape to 127 independent genomic risk loci (160 association signals) and established an autosomal common-variant SNP heritability of h2_SNP = 16.0% on the liability scale. Translating these 127 static statistical signals into pathway-stratified clinical trials requires resolving three quantitative gaps: how the non-APOE polygenic architecture partitions across distinct cellular programs, which effector genes operate via cortical parenchymal versus peripheral myeloid gene expression, and which targets possess nanomolar human bioactivity suitable for genetically stratified trials. Methods: Operating entirely on individual-genotype-free summary statistics structured along a previously established tridimensional diagnostic framework (Axis 1: Etiology and Genetic Architecture; Axis 2: Molecular Pathophysiology and Biomarker Programs; Axis 3: Neuroanatomical-Cognitive Topography; Menendez-Gonzalez, Alzheimers Dement, 2025), we ingested the complete NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog build GCST90695466 (8,159,496 autosomal and 160,704 X-chromosome variants). First, we performed functional heritability partitioning via stratified excess chi-square inflation and additive genetic variance (sum 2pq*beta^2) across +/-50 kb cis-regulatory windows of 50 fine-mapped effector genes organized into five mechanistic Axis 2 programs (MICROGLIAL_IMMUNE, PROTEOPATHY_AUTOPHAGY, ENDOCYTIC_VESICULAR, SYNAPTIC_CALCIUM, and MITOCHONDRIAL_OXIDATIVE). Second, we conducted Summary-data-based Mendelian Randomization (SMR) and Approximate Bayes Factor colocalization (PP.H4) across 54 human tissues in GTEx v10 (4,415 matched cis-eQTLs) alongside Open Targets v4 SuSiE fine-mapped credible sets spanning ROS/MAP dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), BrainSeq, primary human monocytes, and UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project (UKB-PPP) plasma pQTLs. Third, we queried EMBL-EBI ChEMBL v34 across 2,785 human bioactivity assays (IC50, Ki, Kd, EC50) and Open Targets tractability matrices to construct an empirical pharmacogenomic target atlas. Results: Across 8,159,496 autosomal variants, the genome-wide mean test statistic was chi2_GW = 1.5099. Outside the APOE/TOMM40 super-locus (max chi2 = 3,267.15; 2pq*beta^2 = 0.0882, accounting for 74.82% of top-locus additive variance), 89,589 cis-regulatory SNPs across 48 non-APOE effector genes exhibited a 12.88-fold heritability enrichment over the autosomal background. Normalized across the 16.0% polygenic liability scale, non-APOE functional heritability concentrated in MICROGLIAL_IMMUNE (39.22% share; h2_SNP = 6.28%; 13.02x enrichment; mean chi2 = 7.64) and PROTEOPATHY_AUTOPHAGY (36.34% share; h2_SNP = 5.81%; 14.98x enrichment; mean chi2 = 8.64), followed by ENDOCYTIC_VESICULAR (16.71% share; h2_SNP = 2.67%; 12.69x enrichment; mean chi2 = 7.47), SYNAPTIC_CALCIUM (5.40% share; h2_SNP = 0.86%; 10.05x enrichment; mean chi2 = 6.13), and MITOCHONDRIAL_OXIDATIVE (2.33% share; h2_SNP = 0.37%; 5.24x enrichment; mean chi2 = 3.67). Multi-tissue SMR and colocalization resolved a striking divergence between Axis 3 cortical parenchyma and myeloid compartments: QPCT (rs2300880; Z_SMR = -4.62, p_SMR = 3.93e-6, PP.H4_cis = 0.919, PP.H4_local = 0.994 in Brain_Cortex; PP.H4_local = 0.979 in Brain_Frontal_Cortex_BA9) and AXL (rs12979764; p_SMR = 2.13e-4, PP.H4_cis = 0.902, PP.H4_local = 0.924 in Brain_Cortex) colocalized directly within human cerebral cortex and ROS/MAP DLPFC. Conversely, canonical myeloid and endocytic drivers (BIN1, CD33, TREM2, INPP5D, SYK) exhibited near-zero bulk cortical eQTL colocalization (PP.H4_cis <= 0.025 in Brain_Cortex) despite high SuSiE Locus-to-Gene scores (L2G = 0.875-0.968) and robust colocalization in primary monocytes and spleen (INPP5D PP.H4_local = 0.992; BIN1 PP.H4_local = 0.999). ChEMBL v34 bioactivity profiling confirmed low-nanomolar human target potency for clinical-stage compounds across all five programs, including isradipine (2.0 nM) and nilvadipine (19.0 nM) for CACNA1S, omaveloxolone (2.2 nM) for KEAP1, fostamatinib/R406 (41.0 nM) for SYK, and varoglutamstat/PQ912 (61.0 nM) for QPCT. Conclusion: Over three-quarters (75.56%) of the non-APOE common-variant heritability of Alzheimer's disease resides within microglial immune surveillance and proteopathic clearance networks. If prospectively validated in genotype-stratified clinical cohorts, these empirical summary-statistics findings suggest that therapeutic efficacy in sporadic AD may depend on matching pathway-selective drugs to a patient's individual Functional Pathway Burden Score rather than administering uniform monotherapies to genetically unstratified populations.

after.title: Preprint: Epilepsy Lateralization by Elastic Net Regularization of a Diffusion Tensor Imaging Biomarker using Machine Learning
after.authors: Lepping, R. J.; Pearl, M.; Chen, X.; Hu, J.; Li, Y.; Akhter, M.; Farrenburg, M.; Landazuri, P.; Pearson, C. M.
after.abstract: Objective: Accurate lateralization of the epileptogenic focus is essential for presurgical evaluation of patients with drug-resistant epilepsy. This study examined whether diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) measures of white matter microstructure, combined with clinical and demographic variables, could classify epilepsy lateralization using machine learning. Methods: We present a retrospective analysis of 334 adult patients undergoing presurgical epilepsy evaluation at the University of Kansas Health System. Fractional anisotropy (FD) and mean diffusivity (MD) were extracted from 36 bilateral white matter tracts and combined with clinical and demographic variables. Several supervised machine learning approaches were evaluated, with elastic net logistic regression selected for detailed analysis. Models classified right-sided, left-sided, and bilateral or generalized epilepsy. Performance was evaluated with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity as performance metrics. Results: Elastic net models demonstrated good discrimination across classification tasks, with AUC values ranging from 0.76 to 0.88. The strongest performance distinguished left-sided epilepsy from bilateral or generalized epilepsy (AUC = 0.88; accuracy = 0.90; sensitivity = 0.90; specificity = 0.89). Discrimination between unilateral epilepsy and bilateral or generalized epilepsy was also good (AUC = 0.83). Classification of right-sided versus left-sided epilepsy demonstrated lower performance (AUC = 0.76). Significance: DTI-derived white matter features analyzed using a machine learning approach may provide complementary information for epilepsy lateralization during presurgical evaluation. Further studies incorporating other pre-surgical evaluation data into the machine learning model are needed to establish the clinical utility of this approach.

after.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Astrocytic reactivity, measured by plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), is robustly elevated across the Alzheimer disease (AD) continuum, yet its relationship with the amyloid cascade remains poorly understood. METHODS: We integrated plasma GFAP with multimodal AD biomarkers, including cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or plasma amyloid-beta (Abeta42/40), amyloid and tau positron emission tomography (PET), structural MRI, and clinical severity, across a discovery cohort (Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center, n=278) and an independent replication cohort (Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, n=236). RESULTS: In the overall samples of both cohorts, plasma GFAP statistically mediated the associations between soluble Abeta42/40 and amyloid PET and between amyloid PET and tau PET; both remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. In tau-negative individuals, the indirect association between soluble Abeta42/40 and amyloid PET remained significant after correction only in Knight ADRC. In amyloid-positive individuals, the indirect association between amyloid PET and tau PET remained significant after correction only in ADNI. Interaction findings were not consistently replicated across cohorts, either before or after correction. Plasma proteomics identified a GFAP-associated protein network enriched for extracellular matrix and immune-related pathways. DISCUSSION: These findings support associations of plasma GFAP with amyloid and tau biomarkers within A/T-defined groups and identify GFAP-associated extracellular matrix and inflammatory protein signatures that warrant further investigation.

after.title: Preprint: CSF PrP-amyloid seeding predicts clinical onset in inherited prion disease
after.authors: Mok, T. H.; Nihat, A.; Vallabh, S. M.; Noa, B.; Omer, N.; Geschwind, M.; Arnold, S. E.; Minikel, E. V.; Collinge, J.; Mead, S.
after.abstract: Silent proteopathic seed propagation is hypothesised to precede neurodegenerative disease, but direct evidence that it signals near-term clinical conversion in humans is lacking. In prion disease, a prototypic disorder of proteopathic seeding, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) offers a direct measure of prion protein amyloid seeding activity. We analysed longitudinal CSF RT-QuIC data from 94 PRNP E200K mutation carriers across international natural history cohorts to determine whether seeding status predicts clinical conversion. Eleven carriers developed inherited prion disease; all showed at least one positive RT-QuIC result before onset. First positivity appeared a median of 2.0 years prior to symptoms (IQR 1.3-3.3; range 0.2-4.8). Landmark analyses showed RT-QuIC positivity identified a markedly increased short-term conversion risk, whereas persistently asymptomatic carriers remained negative throughout follow-up. These findings establish CSF RT-QuIC positivity as a biomarker-defined state of incipient conversion in E200K carriers, informing risk stratification and preventive trial design.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, USA
after.abstract: Introduction: Olfactory impairment is an early feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, it is unclear if olfactory performance reflects early pathological changes during preclinical AD and/or predicts subsequent clinical progression among characterized cognitively normal (CN) individuals. We aimed to determine whether odor identification differs by amyloid status, relates to medial temporal lobe (MTL) tau burden and morphometry, and predicts longitudinal conversion to mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Methods: We analyzed data from 257 cognitively normal (CN) older adults enrolled in PREVENT-AD (n = 217) and UCLouvain (n = 40), including 76 amyloid-positive (CN A+) and 181 amyloid-negative participants (CN A-). Participants completed olfactory testing, underwent tau-PET imaging, and structural MRI. Results: CN A+ participants had significantly lower odor identification performance than CN A- participants, with no evidence of cohort heterogeneity. Tau-PET associations with odor identification differed by cohort. After whole-brain FDR correction and exclusion of extreme values, parahippocampal tau burden was negatively associated with odor identification score in UCLouvain ([18F]MK-6240), an association that was not found in PREVENT-AD ([18F]flortaucipir). No morphometric association survived multiple comparison correction. In 250 participants with longitudinal follow-up, each 10-percentage-point higher odor identification score was associated with a 16% lower hazard of incident MCI, independent of baseline global cognition and APOE {epsilon}4-carrier status. Discussion: Odor identification was lower in preclinical AD and associated with incident MCI independently of baseline global cognition and APOE {epsilon}4-carrier status. Its association with parahippocampal tau burden differed between cohorts, supporting further investigation using harmonized imaging methods.

after.authors: White, K. P.; Tartar, J. L.; Roel, M.; Dwaraka, V. B.; Chau, M.; Perlmutter, A.; Starratt, V.; Chen, J.; Hewlings, S. J.
after.abstract: Subjective cognitive difficulties are common in midlife and later life, and flavonoid-rich foods may support everyday cognitive function. Tartary buckwheat (Fagopyrum tataricum) sprouts are rich in rutin and other flavonoids, but their cognitive effects have not been tested in humans. In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, US adults with self-reported cognitive difficulties received 18 g per day of Himalayan Tartary buckwheat (HTB) sprout powder or matched placebo for 12 weeks. Of 848 randomized participants, 662 were analyzed. While the rate of change in the primary outcome, PROMIS Cognitive Function, did not differ between arms (contrast = 0.03, 95% CI -0.07 to 0.13; p = .59),PROMIS Cognitive Abilities improved nominally faster with HTB (contrast = 0.12, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.24; p = .046), but not after Bonferroni adjustment. Among participants with final-week data (n = 296), more HTB than placebo participants achieved a meaningful ([≥]0.5 SD) improvement in Cognitive Abilities (68.7% vs 52.5%; RR = 1.32, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.59; p = .003). Fatigue, sleep-related impairment and depressive symptoms did not differ between arms. In exploratory computerized testing (n = 512), HTB participants had faster reaction times on the Flanker and Stroop tasks, without loss of accuracy. Exploratory epigenetic analyses (n = 34) identified hypothesis-generating signals in epigenetic age and immune-cell composition, none surviving multiple-testing correction. Side-effect rates were similar between arms. HTB sprout powder did not improve the primary outcome, but findings for perceived cognitive abilities and processing speed warrant confirmation in adequately powered trials. Trial registration: NCT07245784.

after.authors: Uceda Arias-Stella, E.; Kastner, L.; Copperman, N.; Then, G.; Karlin, J.; Mahant, A.; Crimella, J.; Isakoff, M.; Hayashi, M.; Ewart, M. R.; San Martin, R.; Berg, A.; Gregory, C. A.; Loeb, D.
after.abstract: Background: Dickkopf-1 (DKK1) is a secreted protein that acts as a Wnt antagonist and is implicated in osteosarcoma progression. Elevated circulating DKK1 levels have been described at OS diagnosis, but its circulating dynamics, prognostic relevance, and cellular distribution remain incompletely characterized. Methods: We analysed longitudinal plasma DKK1 in 34 patients using mixed-effects models, evaluated DKK1 expression and survival in two independent transcriptomic cohorts, and examined cellular and tissue distribution using single-cell transcriptomics and immunohistochemistry. Cultured mesenchymal stem cells were assessed as potential nonmalignant sources. Results: Circulating DKK1 declined by 12.4% per 30-day period during treatment, without significant changes detected around primary tumour resection or relapse. Metastatic presentation and poor histologic response were associated with higher estimated DKK1 levels. Higher tumour DKK1 expression was associated with worse overall and metastasis-free survival (pooled HRs per SD increase: 1.35 [95% CI 1.02 - 1.78] and 1.48 [1.06 - 2.07], respectively). DKK1 transcripts were predominantly detected in malignant cells across multiple subpopulations and protein staining was enriched in osteoid and matrix-rich regions of primary tumours. Conclusions: Tumour DKK1 expression is associated with adverse outcomes, while circulating concentration decline over treatment time. These findings support further prognostic evaluation and investigation of the associations among DKK1 expression and production, tissue localisation, and circulating levels.

after.title: Preprint: Accuracy and precision of visual acuity tests: A systematic review and meta-analysis across testing strategies
after.authors: Chen, C.; Browne, A. W.; Skerswetat, J.
after.abstract: Purpose: Visual acuity (VA) testing has expanded from examiner-guided to examinee self-guided assessments, yet measurement variability may limit clinical utility. This meta-analysis investigated VA-test's intertest and test-retest accuracy and precision across different testing strategies. Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched PubMed, Google Scholar, and Scopus for VA validation studies published between 1 January 1983 to 02 December 2024. Eligible studies reported intertest or test-retest Bland-Altman mean bias and limits of agreement (LoA); objective VA assessments and correlation coefficient only studies were excluded. Testing strategies were classified by test site, optotype sampling methods, response input methods, and level of supervision. Accuracy outcomes were reported as mean biases. Precision outcomes were reported as intertest LoA half-width and test-retest coefficient of repeatability (CoR) for test-retest. Multilevel random-effects models accounted for multiple estimates per study. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Results: Across 82 included studies (10,873 participants), pooled intertest and test-retest mean biases were both 0.01 logMAR. Intertest LoA half-width was 0.19 logMAR and test-retest CoR was 0.14 logMAR. Variability showed marginal difference by optotype sampling (adaptive: LoA half-width 0.20 logMAR, CoR 0.15 logMAR; fixed: 0.18, 0.13) or response input method (examiner: 0.19, 0.13; self-run: 0.19, 0.18). Only few studies reported results for test site and level of supervision, hence only intertest was compared (test site, clinic: LoA half-width 0.19 logMAR vs remote 0.27 logMAR and level of supervision, supervised: 0.19 logMAR vs unsupervised 0.26 logMAR). QUADAS-2 identified patient selection as the domain of greatest bias concern. Conclusion: Across testing strategies, VA assessments showed minimal systematic bias but substantial variability. Lack of precision is more notable in remote and unsupervised testing while no difference within optotype sampling and response-input methods. Future development should prioritize on improving precision of visual acuity tests with finer adaptive optotype resolution and remote/unsupervised testings through repeatability studies.

after.authors: Soisangwan, N.; Garimella, K. V.; Schatz, M. C.; Eichler, E. E.; Sedlazeck, F. J.; Talkowski, M. E.; Cunial, F.; Lee, S. K.; All of Us Research Program Long Read Working Group,  ; Hsieh, P.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Genetics, Cell Biology, and Development, University of Minnesota, Twin Cities, MN, USA
after.abstract: Background: Identifying functional variants that influence human health remains a challenge in human genetics. Conventional genotype-phenotype association studies test millions of variants, imposing a substantial multiple-testing burden as genomic and biobank datasets expand in size and variant diversity. Additionally, the contribution of structural variation, which is a substantial driver of genetic diversity, remains underexplored in these studies. Signatures of recent positive selection offer a powerful biological basis for prioritizing potentially functional variation, although demographic history can confound their detection and interpretation in these analyses. Results: We performed evolution-guided association mapping using long-read genomes from 1,027 self-identified Black or African American participants in the All of Us Research Program and short-read genomes from an additional 38,552 matched participants of African-ancestry. Using demography-calibrated inferences, we identified 228 genomic regions with local ancestry enrichment or depletion and 1,616 candidate loci showing putative recent positive selection signals. These loci were enriched for genic and regulatory sequences, as well as previously reported eQTL, sQTL, and GWAS associations. Leveraging the resolution of the long-read data, we mapped 15 structural variants to these candidate loci, including 10 located within 1,000 base pairs of putative cis-regulatory enhancers. Admixture- and selection-based phenome-wide association testing identified 13 and 446 nominal associations, respectively, 17 of which remained significant following replication and meta-analysis. Conclusions: Our results support the use of evolutionary signatures as a robust framework for uncovering clinically relevant variation, including structural variants, in underrepresented populations.

after.title: Preprint: Evaluating uncertainty for detecting performance loss and guiding deferral after model transfer between hospital systems
after.authors: Behling, S.; Schulte-Althoff, M.; Haufe, S.; Grünewald, E.; Balzer, F.; Frey, N.; Boie, S. D.
after.abstract: Clinical prediction models often perform worse after transfer between hospital systems, but deterioration becomes apparent only once outcomes are known. We investigated whether uncertainty measures available at prediction time warn of performance loss and can help identify individual predictions requiring review. Three neural network architectures were trained on MIMIC-IV for in-hospital mortality prediction and evaluated on eICU-CRD. Measures included predictive entropy, mutual information from Monte Carlo dropout and deep ensembles, and representation density. After transfer, AUROC fell from 0.86-0.87 to 0.76-0.77 and calibration worsened, while entropy and mutual information were lower. None of the measures reliably indicated the reduced performance. Deferring the 20% with the highest entropy reduced the remaining error rate from 17.5-20.1% to 6.3-8.0%; the deferred patients included 91-99% of false alarms but only 2-7% of missed deaths, which carried low uncertainty. Uncertainty therefore supported selective review but failed to reveal performance loss.

after.title: Preprint: An Edge-AI Pose-Estimation Platform for Real-Time Posture and Posture-Transition Monitoring: A Feasibility Study for Pre-Emptive Fall-Risk Alerting in Elderly and Dementia Care
after.authors: Sutton, B.; Perry, I.; Kim, L.; Jujjuvarapu, A.; Chae, Y.; Kim, Y.-t.
after.abstract: Falls and unmonitored patient movements remain leading causes of harm in healthcare settings. Current solutions - such as weight-based alarms, remote video monitoring, and in-person sitters - are reactive, labor-intensive, or prone to false alarms, often compromising both care quality and staff efficiency. We developed a machine learning-enabled, proactive-preventive patient monitoring platform that uses 17-keypoint pose estimation to detect changes in patient posture and generate alerts in real time. The Edge-AI device integrates a Raspberry Pi 5, Hailo-8L neural processing unit (NPU), and Raspberry Pi camera module 3, and runs Hailo-YOLOv8-Pose at 30 frames per second to classify postures (i.e., lying, Fowlers, sitting, standing). Alerts are transmitted via Bluetooth to caregivers through earphones or speakers. System performance was evaluated across multiple scenarios, including bed and chair monitoring, free limb movement, partial body occlusion (e.g., blankets), and varying lighting and care environments. The platform maintained accurate monitoring under varying lighting conditions, including lights-off scenarios, and because all processing occurs locally without network dependence, it is designed to continue operating during network outages - an important resilience feature for care environments where connectivity may be interrupted. By abstracting images into skeletal keypoints without recording video, the system preserves privacy while potentially enabling earlier intervention and reducing false alarms and caregiver workload. This cost-effective, scalable system supports future enhancements such as dual alerting, multi-device full-room coverage, and continuous monitoring for dementia patients.

after.title: Preprint: VaccineScout: A Computational Framework for Guiding the Composition and Valency of SARS-CoV-2 Vaccine Updates
after.authors: Gangwar, P.; Khanna, S.; Wertheim, J.; Lin, B.; Turakhia, Y.
after.abstract: The continual evolution of SARS-CoV-2 necessitates periodic vaccine updates to maintain immunity against newly emerging variants. However, vaccine design remains largely guided by experimental serological studies, and there is no publicly available computational framework to help systematically prioritize vaccine variants and guide valency selection. Here, we analyze over 14 million SARS-CoV-2 genomes collected globally between 2021 and 2025 and find that over half of spike amino acid sequences (primary vaccine target) observed during the first six months after vaccine selection were already circulating at the time of selection, compared with only 5-10% of sequences during the subsequent six months. These findings provide quantitative support for annual COVID-19 vaccine updates. We further show that circulating variant prevalence and open-source variant fitness predictors can both effectively rank circulating variants by their future prevalence. Motivated by these findings, we developed VaccineScout, a computational framework that recommends vaccine candidates by minimizing the average spike amino acid substitution distances to the forecasted prevalence of circulating variants. VaccineScout also helps determine vaccine valency by quantifying diminishing returns as additional variants are introduced. Retrospective analyses showed that VaccineScout-recommended candidates either matched U.S. Food and Drug Administration recommendations or had lower average spike sequence distances to future variants and higher fitness. In addition, their spike distances to future variants were comparable to an oracle selection informed by future prevalence, indicating near-optimal performance by this metric. Together, VaccineScout introduces an in silico framework for systematically prioritizing SARS-CoV-2 vaccine candidates for costly downstream experimental validation.

after.title: Preprint: Diagnostic accuracy of a single-reaction, pan-lineage Lassa virus RT-PCR at two Nigerian laboratories: a retrospective and prospective cohort study
after.authors: Adedosu, N. A.; Alhaji, S. Y.; Etafo, J.; Abduljalail, I. I.; Aderibigbe, R. I.; Atu, A. O.; Gbenga-Ayeni, O.; Mikail, B. A.; Uzuajemeh, R. I.; Yarima, A. M.; Njoku-Attah, N.; MacLeod, I. J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Aldatu Biosciences, 313 Pleasant Street, Watertown, MA 02472
after.abstract: Background Lassa virus (LASV) intra- and inter-lineage nucleotide diversity has made it challenging to develop a single-reaction RT-PCR assay that can detect all viral variants with equal sensitivity. We evaluated PANDAA(R) LASV, a single-reaction pan-lineage RT-PCR assay, at two Nigerian Lassa fever laboratories against the RealStar(R) Lassa Virus RT-PCR Kit 2.0, the current diagnostic standard in Nigeria, which requires two separate reactions per patient sample to mitigate against false negative results. Methodology and Principal Findings We conducted a diagnostic accuracy study using retrospectively (n = 200) and prospectively (n = 100) plasma samples that had been collected from patients meeting the standard case definition of suspected Lassa fever for testing by real-time PCR at Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University Teaching Hospital in Bauchi and Federal Medical Centre in Owo. PANDAA LASV(R) sensitivity was 98.6% (138/140; 95% CI 94.9-99.8%), specificity 99.4% (155/156; 96.5-100%), and accuracy 99.0% (293/296; 97.1-99.8%). The positive likelihood ratio was 153.8 (21.8-1084.9) and the negative likelihood ratio 0.01 (0.00-0.06). PANDAA Ct values correlated significantly with the reference assay L gene target (Spearman's {rho} = 0.80; p < 0.0001) and GPC target ({rho} = 0.69; p < 0.0001). Three confirmed discordant results occurred at high Ct values near assay detection limits. Performance was consistent across sites with overlapping confidence intervals for sensitivity and specificity and no difference in median Ct values for any assay target between laboratories. Ct values were significantly lower in patients [≥] 45 years (p = 0.008). Conclusions and Significance PANDAA(R) LASV demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy to detect Lassa virus RNA compared to the dual-reaction reference assay. Reducing the operational burden from two PCR reactions per sample to a single PANDAA(R) LASV reaction while maintaining equivalent sensitivity and specificity could have a direct impact on labour and reagent costs, and turnaround time. Clinical validation against additional LASV lineages is an immediate priority.

after.title: Preprint: Physiological Waveform Features Based Aging Clocks Associate with Cardiovascular Disease
after.authors: Pal, R.; Barney, A.; Cannesson, M.
after.abstract: Aging affects the morphology of photoplethysmography (PPG) and arterial blood pressure (ABP) waveforms. Here, we demonstrate that machine learning (ML) models trained on features derived from PPG or ABP waveforms can predict an individual's age. We further investigated whether the discrepancy between predicted and chronological age (Age-Gap) could serve as a measure of cardiovascular health by testing its association with cardiovascular disease (CVD). From a large perioperative dataset of 17,327 surgical patients, high-fidelity PPG and ABP waveforms were analyzed, and over 840 time-, frequency-, and statistical-domain features per cardiac cycle were extracted using a signal-processing-based tool. These features were then used to develop ML-based aging clocks, PPGAge and ABPAge, trained on PPG and ABP features, respectively. For each aging clock, we evaluated five ML models: Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest, Lasso, and Elastic Net. Individuals were classified as having accelerated, normal, or delayed aging based on their Age-Gap relative to the model-specific mean absolute error (MAE, rounded up to the nearest whole year): accelerated aging was defined as Age-Gap [≥] +MAE, normal aging as -MAE [≤] Age-Gap < +MAE, and delayed aging as Age-Gap < -MAE. LightGBM provided the best age predictions for both aging clocks, with Pearson correlation coefficients (r) of 0.92 and 0.92 and R-squared values of 0.81 and 0.82 for PPGAge and ABPAge, respectively. Moreover, we found that accelerated aging was significantly associated with higher odds of CVD for both aging clocks, PPGAge (odds ratio, 1.87 [95% CI, 1.59-2.21], p<0.001) and ABPAge (odds ratio, 2.28 [95% CI, 1.51-3.43], p<0.001). Additionally, delayed aging was significantly associated with lower odds of CVD for PPGAge (odds ratio, 0.68 [95% CI, 0.58-0.80], p<0.001). Our findings suggest that aging clocks based on high-fidelity PPG or ABP waveform features may serve as novel biomarkers for identifying individuals with higher odds of CVD.

We further investigated whether the discrepancy between predicted and chronological age (Age-Gap) could serve as a measure of cardiovascular health by testing its association with cardiovascular disease (CVD). From a large perioperative dataset of 17,327 surgical patients, high-fidelity PPG and ABP waveforms were analyzed, and over 840 time-, frequency-, and statistical-domain features per cardiac cycle were extracted using a signal-processing-based tool. These features were then used to develop ML-based aging clocks, PPGAge and ABPAge, trained on PPG and ABP features, respectively. For each aging clock, we evaluated five ML models: Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest, Lasso, and Elastic Net. Individuals were classified as having accelerated, normal, or delayed aging based on their Age-Gap relative to the model-specific mean absolute error (MAE, rounded up to the nearest whole year): accelerated aging was defined as Age-Gap [≥] +MAE, normal aging as -MAE [≤] Age-Gap < +MAE, and delayed aging as Age-Gap < -MAE. LightGBM provided the best age predictions for both aging clocks, with Pearson correlation coefficients (r) of 0.92 and 0.92 and R-squared values of 0.81 and 0.82 for PPGAge and ABPAge, respectively. Moreover, we found that accelerated aging was significantly associated with higher odds of CVD for both aging clocks, PPGAge (odds ratio, 1.87 [95% CI, 1.59-2.21], p<0.001) and ABPAge (odds ratio, 2.28 [95% CI, 1.51-3.43], p<0.001). Additionally, delayed aging was significantly associated with lower odds of CVD for PPGAge (odds ratio, 0.68 [95% CI, 0.58-0.80], p<0.001). Our findings suggest that aging clocks based on high-fidelity PPG or ABP waveform features may serve as novel biomarkers for identifying individuals with higher odds of CVD.

after.title: Preprint: Interpretable ECG manifolds link longitudinal electrical phenotypes to heart-failure risk in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
after.authors: Cerveri, P.; Taconne, M. H.; Corino, V.; Mainardi, L.
after.abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) produces heterogeneous electrical phenotypes whose continuous organization, longitudinal evolution and clinical relevance remain poorly defined. We developed complementary variational-autoencoder representations to map HCM ECG morphology relative to physiological variation and characterize within-subject change. Using 5,194 normal-reference ECGs and 2,594 longitudinal visits from 650 individuals with HCM, we found that HCM overlapped the physiological manifold but extended towards its periphery, while an HCM-oriented manifold largely reorganized shared electrical modes. Mixed-effects models identified longitudinal drift in selected phenotypic axes. A lateral/frontal QRS-force coordinate remained time-dependent after censoring septal reduction therapy, atrial fibrillation and pacing, and lower values were associated with subsequent heart-failure risk in baseline and time-updated analyses. A time-conditioned change VAE identified four interpretable within-subject modes aligned with longer-term trajectories. Sarcomeric genotype was associated with phenotype position but not trajectory rate.

after.title: Preprint: Before AI tells patients what to eat, it needs to know where they live: a cross-sectional ecological study of diabetes and food access in California and Michigan census tracts, with a spotlight on Metro Detroit and Metro Los Angeles
after.authors: Chitipolu, S. S.
after.abstract: Background: AI chatbots now give people with diabetes diet advice, but whether those foods can be bought near home is rarely checked. Methods: In a cross-sectional ecological study of 11,974 California and Michigan census tracts, I linked diabetes prevalence (CDC PLACES 2025) with two USDA food-access maps: all SNAP-authorized stores (2025) and large grocery stores only (2019). I identified double-burden tracts (high diabetes and low income/low access) and hidden food deserts (low access to large grocery stores, but not to any SNAP store). In a pilot, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude generated meal plans for the same person across 20 high-diabetes tracts in Metro Los Angeles and Metro Detroit; I scored whether advice was healthy and whether foods were sold at nearby store types. Results: Double-burden tracts were few (71 in California, 19 in Michigan), almost none in the two metros. Food-desert tracts had a 1.5 percentage-point higher diabetes prevalence (95% CI, 1.0-2.0). Counting all SNAP stores hid 567 Californian and 329 Michigan food deserts; in Metro Detroit, all 97 disappeared, including 51 high-diabetes tracts with about 19,500 adults with diabetes. Chatbot advice was healthy, but in hidden tracts 30% of recommended foods were not reliably sold nearby; the chatbots barely adjusted. Of 55 places they named, 13% had errors, and most were over a mile away. Conclusions: The current USDA map obscures food deserts, especially in Detroit, and AI diet advice barely adjusts for them. AI nutrition tools for diabetes should include a place-aware check built on public food-access data.

after.title: Preprint: Estimating duration in sex work from cross-sectional studies: a Bayesian global synthesis suggests shorter durations
after.authors: Knight, J.; Wang, S.; Wang, L.; Mishra, S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: 1) MAP Centre for Urban Health Solutions, Unity Health Toronto
after.abstract: Durations selling sex are key determinants of HIV/STI transmission dynamics and service coverage. Such durations are usually estimated from cross-sectional surveys of people actively selling sex. However, cross-sectional surveys are more likely to include individuals selling sex for longer, and survey-reported durations will be right-censored. Prior works have not adequately addressed these two competing biases. In this paper, we derive the mathematical relationship between the distribution of durations reported in cross-sectional surveys and the distribution of true durations in the population overall. These distributions will be identical if true durations are exponentially distributed; otherwise, reported durations will typically underestimate the variance in true durations. We develop a parametric Bayesian model of this relationship, and apply it to re-analyze aggregate data from a global systematic review. Our model-estimated average true durations selling sex are significantly shorter than previously published for all regions - e.g. in Africa: 2.1 (95% CI: 1.8-2.5) versus 5.5 years; in Asia: 1.4 (1.2-1.5) versus 2.8-4.0 years. Shorter average durations then suggest that HIV incidence in sex work could be higher than previously thought, to match the same HIV prevalence data. Our approach can be applied beyond sex work, to characterize duration distributions for any transient risk/disease state.
